title: 2 Chronicles 7:1–10
context: 2 Chronicles 7:1–10 completes the dedication of the temple. When Solomon finishes praying, fire comes down from heaven and consumes the offerings, and the LORD’s glory fills the house so that the priests cannot enter. The people bow with their faces to the ground and give thanks, saying that the LORD is good and his loving kindness endures forever. Solomon and the people offer huge numbers of sacrifices, the Levites play the instruments David made, and Solomon hallows the middle of the court because the bronze altar is too small. The feast lasts seven days, followed by a solemn assembly, and the people go home joyful on the twenty-third day of the seventh month. The parallel in 1 Kings 8:62–66 gives the same sacrifice numbers but does not mention fire from heaven; it describes the feast as seven days and seven more, and says the people were sent away on the eighth day. Compare also the fire at the first offerings of the tabernacle in Leviticus 9:24. These notes name the differences without harmonizing them. Arminian and Reformed readers share the central reading: God graciously accepts the worship of his people and makes his presence known among them.

verses.text: Now when Solomon had finished praying, fire came down from heaven and consumed the burnt offering and the sacrifices; and the LORD’s glory filled the house.
verses.arminianNotes: When Solomon finishes praying, fire comes from heaven, consumes the offerings, and the LORD’s glory fills the house. Arminian readers see God answering a prayer offered in faith and publicly showing his acceptance of the temple and its worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress that the fire and glory are God’s own work, confirming the place he chose. Both traditions note the parallel with Leviticus 9:24 and that 1 Kings 8 does not mention the fire, and they name that difference without harmonizing it.

verses.text: The priests could not enter into the LORD’s house, because the LORD’s glory filled the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: The priests cannot enter because the LORD’s glory fills the house. Arminians see the overwhelming holiness of God’s presence, which even the appointed priests could not approach at that moment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and compare the scene with the glory filling the tabernacle in Exodus 40:34–35 and the temple in 2 Chronicles 5:13–14. Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about God’s holy presence among his people.

verses.text: All the children of Israel looked on, when the fire came down, and the LORD’s glory was on the house. They bowed themselves with their faces to the ground on the pavement, worshiped, and gave thanks to the LORD, saying, “For he is good, for his loving kindness endures forever!”
verses.arminianNotes: The people see the fire and glory, bow to the ground, worship, and give thanks that the LORD is good and his loving kindness endures forever. Arminian readers see a fitting response of humble worship from the whole nation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the refrain of God’s enduring loving kindness as central to Israel’s worship (compare Psalm 136). Both traditions read the people’s response as a model of reverence and thanksgiving in God’s presence.

verses.text: Then the king and all the people offered sacrifices before the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The king and all the people offer sacrifices before the LORD. Arminians see the whole community taking part in worship, not just the king and priests, which shows the shared response of God’s people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the sacrifices as worship offered according to God’s appointed way. Both traditions read the verse as a transition to the large numbers of offerings in the next verse.

verses.text: King Solomon offered a sacrifice of twenty-two thousand head of cattle and a hundred twenty thousand sheep. So the king and all the people dedicated God’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon offers twenty-two thousand cattle and a hundred twenty thousand sheep, and the king and people dedicate God’s house. Arminian readers see lavish worship expressing gratitude, and they note that 1 Kings 8:63 gives the same numbers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the abundance of offerings as fitting for a moment of great blessing. Both traditions read the verse as recording the dedication of the temple to God’s service, which is shared ground.

verses.text: The priests stood, according to their positions; the Levites also with instruments of music of the LORD, which David the king had made to give thanks to the LORD, when David praised by their ministry, saying “For his loving kindness endures forever.” The priests sounded trumpets before them; and all Israel stood.
verses.arminianNotes: The priests and Levites stand in their places, the Levites play the instruments David made, praising God’s enduring loving kindness, and the priests sound trumpets. Arminians see ordered worship that combines sacrifice and song.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note the Chronicler’s emphasis on David’s arrangements for worship (1 Chronicles 23–25). Both traditions read the verse as showing worship carried out with joy and in good order, without dispute.

verses.text: Moreover Solomon made the middle of the court that was before the LORD’s house holy; for there he offered the burnt offerings and the fat of the peace offerings, because the bronze altar which Solomon had made was not able to receive the burnt offering, the meal offering, and the fat.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon hallows the middle of the court for offerings because the bronze altar is too small. Arminian readers see a practical solution that allowed the people’s abundant worship to be received, and they note the parallel in 1 Kings 8:64.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the king acting to make room for the offerings. Both traditions read the verse as a detail showing the scale of the dedication, and they avoid building doctrine on the arrangement.

verses.text: So Solomon held the feast at that time for seven days, and all Israel with him, a very great assembly, from the entrance of Hamath to the brook of Egypt.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon holds the feast for seven days with all Israel, from the entrance of Hamath to the brook of Egypt. Arminians see a gathering of the whole nation, from its northern to its southern borders, united in worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the wide gathering as a sign of God’s blessing on the united kingdom. Both traditions note the parallel with 1 Kings 8:65 and read the feast as an expression of national joy.

verses.text: On the eighth day, they held a solemn assembly; for they kept the dedication of the altar seven days, and the feast seven days.
verses.arminianNotes: On the eighth day they hold a solemn assembly, having kept the dedication of the altar for seven days and the feast for seven days. Arminian readers see an extended time of worship, and they note that 1 Kings 8:65–66 describes the timing in different words.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and name the difference without harmonizing it. Both traditions read the verse as showing that the dedication and the feast together formed a long season of celebration.

verses.text: On the twenty-third day of the seventh month, he sent the people away to their tents, joyful and glad of heart for the goodness that the LORD had shown to David, to Solomon, and to Israel his people.
verses.arminianNotes: On the twenty-third day of the seventh month Solomon sends the people home joyful for the goodness the LORD had shown to David, Solomon, and Israel. Arminians see joy as the natural fruit of God’s goodness experienced in worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that Chronicles adds Solomon to the list of those who received God’s goodness, while 1 Kings 8:66 names David and Israel. Both traditions read the verse as celebrating God’s faithfulness to his promises.
